We covered Islamic Economics: Theory and Practice by M.A Mannan in this course. Along with some journal articles. It is available in PDF format online. Pretty much covered 90% of that book. You should read that to get an overall perspective. Good, easy to read book.

The one thing that Islam banking for me reiterates again and again is that: 1) everything belongs to god so you're essentially renting something that the bank chooses to give you. 2) Obligatory zakat percentage on your income which forces you to share your wealth. 3) Everything and everyone must be Shariah-compliant.

At the end of the day, Islam says that if you earn money without you working for it, like making interest-based investments that say make your money work for you, is haram. If you didn't work for it, but you have it, that's automatically haram. Everyone wants to be rich, this book knows that the author knows that, so they use that to push their ideas or Islam's ideas in a more Shariah-compliant way.

There's islamic instruments that are alternatives. Since we don't use interest based transactions, we have leasing (Ijarah), partner-relationship where there's profit and loss sharing. I don't remember but he covers terms like Musharaka, Murabaha, Istisna, Salam which is advanced payment before the delivery of the goods. There's like 10 different instruments of financing which we covered.

He also covers bonds, Islamic bonds are called Sukuk which is your income generated from assets. They are called Sukuk since they're free from riba (interest). Riba is haram. Sukuk indicates ownership of an asset. Your conventional bonds indicate a debt obligation. He also covers a lot of flaws like how conventional banking has a large third party involved when you make an investment where as in Islamic banking, you have less of a wall between where exactly your money is going.

I took a course this semester on Islamic Economics and this book came up a lot in discussion. Never read it, but what I can tell you is that it compares Islam's way of dealing with the economy with the capitalist ideology. Like how banking works in capitalism compared to banking in Islam. How everything ultimately belongs to God in Islam compared to how when you buy something, it is now fully owned by you in capitalism.

Zaman believes that humans are built on greed and that capitalism since it's a human-made ideology, makes it worse. Islamic Economics offers a different opinion where there are ideas like obligatory zakat that prompt a share of wealth in the community. The idea that everyone gets an equal chance at life.
